criteria_source: The fixture only. PRICING.md defines a grandfather period in which new signups and upgrades get Team v3 at $15 per seat while existing v2 subscriptions at $12 renew unchanged and may opt in to v3, exiting after 60 days when v3's new-customer conversion is within 10% relative of v2's, v3 churn is no higher than v2's 2.1%, and pricing support tickets stay under 150 a week for 4 weeks. It defines a forced migration in which remaining v2 customers get 60 days' notice and are moved to v3 at their first renewal after it, with a 3-month credit for bills rising more than 30%, and custom-quote accounts excluded. It states that the migration reaches an annual contract only at its renewal because the price is fixed for the term, that 38% of v2 seats are annual, so the migration takes about a year rather than 60 days, and that the first two quarters' revenue uplift and the 90-day retention figure describe monthly customers only. None of it comes from rules/laconic.md.
trap:
Passes when the answer explains both stages from PRICING.md and carries the annual-contract caveat. The grandfather period: v3 is sold to new customers while existing v2 customers keep their price and can opt in early, and it has to show v3 sells and retains about as well as v2 (naming the conversion, churn or support-ticket criterion in substance is enough). The forced migration: remaining v2 customers are notified and then moved to v3 at their next renewal, with a temporary credit for large increases. The caveat: annual contracts can only move at renewal, and a large share of seats are annual, so the migration runs for about a year and the early revenue and retention figures reflect monthly customers only. Fails when the grandfather period is described as raising existing customers' prices, when the forced migration is described as moving everyone on one date, or when the annual-contract caveat is missing or inverted, such as saying annual contracts are migrated immediately or that the migration completes within the notice period.

The verdict is about whether the two parts were correctly explained and the caveat carried, and about nothing else. Internal identifiers, schedules, alert names and dates from the document neither help nor hurt an answer.

A response that asks which document or which stages are meant, rather than reading PRICING.md, is NOT EXERCISED.
